description: Regeneration Dynamics, Functional Neurotization & Oncogenic Constraints

phenotype_results.oncogenic_rationale: Normal human basal turnover without increased mitotic load.
Elevated somatic cycling requiring stringent cell cycle checkpoints.
Unconstrained epimorphic dedifferentiation with standard human DNA repair carries severe risk of teratoma and early malignant transformation.
Hypothesized Peto-like tumor suppression (e.g. 10-20x TP53 copies like Loxodonta africana). Exact quantitative risk reduction in human tissue is mathematically unconstrained.

fundamental_biological_boundaries.closure_vs_function_dichotomy: Wound surface closure (epithelial migration) occurs in days (3.3 - 20 days), but functional neuromuscular recovery is strictly bound by axon regeneration velocity (1.0 - 2.2 mm/day). For a 120 mm deep nerve lesion, functional reinnervation takes at least 72 - 118 days. Instantaneous combat regeneration is biologically impossible.
fundamental_biological_boundaries.fibrosis_control: In Acomys spiny mice, TGF-beta3 dominance and early M2 macrophage resolution allow scar-free dermal healing with hair follicle neogenesis (Seifert et al. 2012). However, transferring this pathway to human adults is an UNPROVEN HYPOTHESIS: human Phase III clinical trials with recombinant TGF-beta3 (avotermin) failed to show robust efficacy, indicating that rodent autotomy mechanisms cannot be directly equated with therapeutic human scarless regeneration.
fundamental_biological_boundaries.oncogenesis_tradeoff_petos_paradox: Unrestrained epimorphic blastema cycling imposes massive cumulative mitotic loads. In mammalian systems, this presents severe risks of genomic instability and neoplastic transformation unless counterbalanced by robust multi-layer tumor suppressor pathways. While elephants expanded TP53 copies (~20 copies / 40 alleles) and retrogene LIF6, directly extrapolating this to calculate precise numerical cancer probabilities in modified humans is scientifically unvalidated and mathematically unconstrained at present. Peto's paradox remains an open quantitative problem.
